historical_timeline.summary: Born Martha Canary near Princeton, Missouri.
Her mother dies in Montana Territory and her father in Utah; she is orphaned at about eleven.
Works in Wyoming railroad camps and military posts; later drives ox teams and hauls wood; often wears men's clothing.
Joins the Black Hills expedition; known as Calamity Jane by 1876; travels to Deadwood in a train that includes Hickok, who is killed that August.
Heavy drinking reported in newspapers; arrests for intoxication.
Nurses sick people during a smallpox epidemic in the Black Hills.
A son dies soon after birth; a daughter is born in 1887; newspapers report that a partner beat her.
Moves from town to town in poverty, at one time living in a pest house.
Tours with a dime museum show; her ghostwritten pamphlet is published.
Taken ill without money and cared for at the Gallatin County poor farm in Bozeman.
A visiting writer finds her aged beyond her years.
Taken to the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo; returns west late in the year.
Dies in Terry, South Dakota; buried in Deadwood.

claims.statement: Her family moved to the Montana gold camps about 1864; in December 1864 a Virginia City newspaper reported the Canary girls destitute. Her mother died at Blackfoot City, Montana Territory, in 1866 and her father in Utah in 1867, leaving her an orphan of about eleven with younger brothers and sisters.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the early bereavement and childhood poverty in the trauma-informed history; the parents' causes of death are not recorded in the cited sources.

She often wore men's clothing, including buckskins.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Severe alcohol use disorder in a woman living in rural poverty: a 44-year-old who does odd jobs and moves between towns comes to a clinic a few weeks after a stay on a county poor farm. The episode covers a nonjudgmental, trauma-informed assessment with the AUDIT, DSM-5-TR criteria and PEth, withdrawal risk with the PAWSS and CIWA-Ar, outpatient withdrawal management with daily checks under the ASAM guideline, parenteral thiamine, electrolytes and nutrition, naltrexone under the APA guideline and the change to a monthly injection when daily pills are hard to keep, liver assessment with FIB-4 and transient elastography, depressive symptoms judged after weeks without alcohol, a structured safety assessment with firearm storage and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, peer recovery support and mutual-help choices, harm reduction and a return to drinking met without blame, the ways alcohol harms women more, and help with housing, food, income and health coverage through real public programs.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Canary returns one week after intake and is seen by Dr. Two Bulls-Harmon of addiction medicine on the same day. Her last drink was on the morning of her intake visit. The clinic nurse saw or called her every day: her CIWA-Ar was 10 on the second day with tremor, sweats and poor sleep, then fell each day to 2 today. She took the five-day gabapentin schedule as written and finished it three days ago, had the three thiamine injections, and took the potassium for five days and the magnesium as prescribed. She has had no seizures, hallucinations or confusion. Her friend stayed close during the worst days. She is eating more. The intake tests showed no HIV or hepatitis C, no hepatitis B infection or immunity, a urine test with no opioids, fentanyl or other drugs, and a negative pregnancy test. The community health worker helped her apply for Medicaid and SNAP, and she has met the peer recovery specialist once. She would like to stay off alcohol completely and wants to know about medicines that help.

She has not had a drink, though she said the pain made her think of whiskey, and a man in town offered her some of his prescription pain pills, which she turned down. She asked whether she could take something stronger for the pain.

consultant_note.history: Ms. Canary, a 44-year-old woman who does odd jobs and moves between towns, is seen at the request of Dr. Kessler one week after starting outpatient withdrawal management. She has drunk heavily for most of her adult life and has tried to stop many times on her own. Her last drink was a week ago. With gabapentin, thiamine and daily nurse checks, her withdrawal peaked at a CIWA-Ar of 10 on the second day and is now over. She wants to stop drinking altogether, does not want to be lectured, and would rather not take a pill every day if there is another way. She has a friend who supports her and has met the clinic's peer recovery specialist
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Kessler's intake note and safety assessment; the nurse's daily CIWA-Ar scores (10 at most, 2 today). AUDIT 31, PEth 820 ng/mL, PHQ-9 14, GAD-7 11 and PC-PTSD-5 2 at intake. Intake laboratory results: AST 96, ALT 44 and GGT 240 U/L, albumin 3.4 g/dL, bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL, INR 1.0, platelets 162, MCV 103 fL; FIB-4 3.93. Today potassium 3.9 mmol/L and magnesium 1.8 mg/dL after replacement. HIV and hepatitis C negative; hepatitis B not infected and not immune; urine drug test negative for opioids, fentanyl and other drugs; pregnancy test negative

exam.finding: Soft and non-tender; liver edge not palpable

assessment.assessment: Nine DSM-5-TR criteria, including craving, failed attempts to cut down, use despite harm to her health and her work, tolerance and withdrawal: a severe disorder. Her long drinking began in a childhood of loss and poverty, and it is met here with treatment, not blame

With a PAWSS of 3, no past seizures or delirium, a support person and daily checks, ambulatory management was appropriate under the ASAM guideline, and gabapentin was a reasonable choice for mild withdrawal in a woman likely to be alone at times and with raised liver tests. Withdrawal is now complete

Naltrexone is a first-line choice under the APA guideline and suits her goal of stopping. Her AST is under three times the upper limit and she has no signs of cirrhosis or hepatitis, so it can be used with liver tests rechecked. The monthly extended-release injection removes the need for a daily pill and suits a woman who moves between places. Acamprosate is the alternative if naltrexone cannot be used; disulfiram is not advised with her liver tests and without someone to supervise doses. She takes no opioids, and the urine test confirms it

assessment.display: Raised liver enzymes with a high FIB-4
assessment.assessment: An AST twice the ALT with a high GGT and macrocytosis fits alcohol-associated liver injury. A FIB-4 above 2.67 needs transient elastography; done after a few weeks without alcohol, it is less likely to be falsely raised by inflammation. Bilirubin, albumin, INR and platelets show no sign of liver failure

Depressive symptoms during heavy drinking often improve within two to four weeks of stopping. With no suicidal thoughts and a safety plan in place, reassessment with the PHQ-9 at about four weeks is reasonable before deciding on an antidepressant

assessment.display: Recovery, harm reduction and social needs
assessment.assessment: Recovery is likelier with housing, food and someone to call. Peer support and a mutual-help group of her choice, including women-only options, help many women. Women develop liver damage after less drinking and fewer years than men, and alcohol raises breast cancer risk; she should hear this plainly. A plan for a return to drinking keeps her safe and in care

safe_messaging_review.notes: Substance use claims, the losses of her children and the reported violence are marked sensitive and recorded once each, plainly and without detail; person-first language; her drinking is described without blame or sensational language. Her clothing and work are documented social history, not a medical matter, and no gender identity is assigned. No relative or companion is named in the modern episode. The safety assessment gives the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and covers firearm storage.
